topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Estimating answers (age 7+)
topic.description: Estimate and read time with increasing accuracy to the nearest minute; record and compare time in terms of seconds, minutes, and hours
evidence: Read an analogue clock to the nearest minute
Estimate how long an activity takes in minutes or seconds
Compare two durations and determine which is longer
topic.assessmentPrompt: If a TV show starts at 5:17 p.m. and ends at 5:43 p.m., can {{name}} work out how long it lasted — and express that in minutes?

pedagogy.summary: Children read an analogue clock to the exact minute AND develop a felt sense of how long seconds, minutes and hours are — estimating durations and comparing them, recording time in each unit. The estimation and comparison strands carry the documented difficulties: children count seconds far too fast, so estimates are wildly short, and they compare bare numbers ignoring units ('30 seconds is longer than 20 minutes because 30 > 20'). Choosing a sensible unit for an event is also hard.
bestPractices: Pair precise reading (count on from the last five) with hands-on estimation ('put your hand up when you think a minute has passed') checked against a real stopwatch
Calibrate seconds vs minutes physically so the child FEELS the difference in scale
Always compare durations in a COMMON unit; make the units explicit before comparing sizes
Match events to sensible units (a blink = seconds, a lesson = minutes/an hour)
Use a stopwatch to connect estimate -> measured value -> comparison
keyRepresentations: Analogue clock with a minute scale (reading on)
Stopwatch / timer for estimating and measuring
A bar or number line to compare durations in a common unit
Everyday events sorted by their natural unit
commonMisconceptions: Counts seconds in the head too quickly, so estimates are badly short
Compares numbers without reference to units (30 seconds > 20 minutes because 30 > 20)
Chooses the wrong unit for an event (seconds for a lesson, hours for a blink)
Thinks a later finish time means a longer duration (carried from earlier duration confusion)
Reads to the nearest minute by counting single minutes from the 12

learn.summary: Year 3 children (age 7–8) learn to read an analogue clock to the nearest minute AND build a felt sense of how long seconds, minutes and hours actually are — estimating real durations, comparing them, and choosing sensible units for events. The hard parts are: estimating (children tend to count seconds in their head far too fast, so estimates come out wildly short), comparing (they compare bare numbers while ignoring units, e.g. '30 seconds is longer than 20 minutes because 30 > 20'), and selecting an appropriate unit for an event. Precise reading should be paired with hands-on calibration against a real timer and with comparisons laid out in a common unit.

activities.title: Tap when you think the time has passed — then reveal the real elapsed time
feedback: If the child tapped at ~10 seconds for 30 seconds: 'Had a whole 30 seconds really gone? Let's check the stopwatch — you tapped early. Try counting one-Mississippi, two-Mississippi.'
When the estimate lands in a sensible range (not at ~10 seconds): 'That's much closer to a real 30 seconds.'
Frame this as rehearsing a steady pace, not a concept to re-explain.
activities.rationale: The too-fast internal counter is a felt performance skill; a live estimate-then-reveal loop against a real measured value makes the error visible and gives immediate calibration feedback. White Rose documents the 'put your hand up when you think a minute/40 seconds has passed' activity checked against a stopwatch. A stopwatch is one way to supply the measured value; an adult timing by hand serves the same purpose.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y3 Time (Steps 10-12) documents that when estimating children often count seconds in their head too quickly, and when comparing they compare numbers without reference to units ('30 seconds is longer than 20 minutes because 30 > 20') and find it hard to choose the correct unit for an event; the recommended activity is 'put your hand up when you think a minute/40 seconds has passed' checked against a stopwatch.
Year 3 pupils should 'estimate and read time with increasing accuracy to the nearest minute; record and compare time in terms of seconds, minutes and hours'.
learnerActions: Close your eyes (or watch a blank screen) and tap/raise a hand when you think 30 seconds has passed.
Compare the moment you tapped with the real elapsed time measured on a stopwatch or timer.
Notice the gap between your tap and the real time — many children tap early for a 30-second estimate because they count too fast in their head, so check whether that happened for you.
Try again, practising a steady 'one-Mississippi' counting pace, and re-estimate to see if your tap gets closer.
Repeat for a minute and for 40 seconds.
activities.intendedInsight: My internal counting can run faster than real seconds; estimating duration is a felt skill I can calibrate against a real timer by checking my tap against the measured time.

activities.title: Compare two durations on one common-unit scale
feedback: If the child picks 30 seconds: 'How many seconds are in 20 minutes? Convert both to seconds, then compare — 20 minutes is 1200 seconds, so 20 minutes is longer.'
For 90s vs 2 minutes: 'Is 90 seconds longer or shorter than 2 minutes? 90 is bigger than 2, but is a second bigger than a minute? Convert: 2 minutes = 120 seconds, so 2 minutes is longer.'
Reinforce: don't compare numbers without their units; make the units explicit before comparing sizes.
activities.rationale: Children apply whole-number reasoning to time and treat quantities as bare counting numbers; laying both durations on a single common-unit scale makes the unit explicit and visible so size can be compared fairly. The dragging-onto-a-shared-line interaction is an optional mechanism; a drawn bar or number line on paper serves the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Children apply discrete whole-number reasoning to time and struggle to coordinate its non-standard groupings, so they treat time quantities like ordinary counting numbers rather than reasoning about the units — consistent with comparing 30 and 20 without regard to seconds vs minutes.

White Rose Y3 Time (Steps 10-12) documents that when estimating children often count seconds in their head too quickly, and when comparing they compare numbers without reference to units ('30 seconds is longer than 20 minutes because 30 > 20') and find it hard to choose the correct unit for an event; the recommended activity is 'put your hand up when you think a minute/40 seconds has passed' checked against a stopwatch.
learnerActions: Take two durations, '30 seconds' and '20 minutes', and place them as bars onto ONE shared number line marked in a common unit (e.g. seconds).
See that 20 minutes = 1200 seconds towers over the 30-second sliver.
State which is longer and say WHY: a minute is 60 seconds, so 20 minutes is 1200 seconds, which is longer than 30 seconds even though 20 is less than 30.
Try more pairs, including a tricky one: 90 seconds vs 2 minutes (90 > 2, but 90s < 120s, so 2 minutes is longer).
activities.intendedInsight: Durations can only be compared fairly when expressed in the same unit; the bare number alone does not tell you which is longer.

activities.title: Read an analogue clock to the exact minute by counting on from the last five
feedback: If the child taps round the dial one minute at a time from the 12: 'Which five has the hand just passed? Start there and count on.'
When they count on from 35: 'Good — 35 plus 3 more is 38.'
Rehearse with the fives marked so the anchor is easy to find.
activities.rationale: Counting single minutes from the 12 is slow and error-prone; anchoring on the last five-minute mark the hand has passed and counting on supports accurate reading to the nearest minute, a statutory Year 3 expectation. The counting-on method is drawn from the scheme-of-learning pedagogy rather than quoted verbatim from a source claim.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'estimate and read time with increasing accuracy to the nearest minute; record and compare time in terms of seconds, minutes and hours'.
learnerActions: Look at a clock showing 2:38.
Find which five the minute hand has just passed (the 35).
Count on from there to the exact minute (+3 to reach 38).
Read the time to the nearest minute and explain the counting-on method.
Rehearse with the five-minute marks shown on the clock face.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading to the exact minute is efficient when I anchor on the last five and count on, rather than counting single minutes from the 12.

activities.title: Match events to sensible units using benchmarks
feedback: If the child says lunch takes '30 seconds' or '5 hours': 'Think of your benchmark — a minute is about a short song. Is lunch closer to a clap, a song, or a whole lesson?'
When a sensible unit is chosen (e.g. minutes for lunch): 'Yes — lunch is many minutes, not seconds.'
A sorting activity can check and build this classification but does not itself produce the felt sense of a duration — pair it with the timed estimation work.
activities.rationale: Choosing the correct unit is documented as hard; building concrete referents gives children something to compare each event against instead of guessing.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y3 Time (Steps 10-12) documents that when estimating children often count seconds in their head too quickly, and when comparing they compare numbers without reference to units ('30 seconds is longer than 20 minutes because 30 > 20') and find it hard to choose the correct unit for an event; the recommended activity is 'put your hand up when you think a minute/40 seconds has passed' checked against a stopwatch.
Year 3 pupils should 'estimate and read time with increasing accuracy to the nearest minute; record and compare time in terms of seconds, minutes and hours'.
learnerActions: Anchor each unit to a familiar benchmark: a second ≈ one clap, a minute ≈ a short song, an hour ≈ a lesson.
Sort everyday events against these benchmarks (a blink, brushing teeth, eating lunch, sleeping overnight).
Choose whether each event is best measured in seconds, minutes or hours, and justify by comparing to the benchmark.
Catch mismatches such as 'lunch takes 30 seconds' or 'a blink takes hours'.
activities.intendedInsight: Each unit has a felt size; I pick the unit for an event by comparing it to a benchmark I know.

activities.title: Sequence and compare durations
feedback: If a sequence is ordered by bare number (placing 90 seconds as the longest, above 2 minutes and even 1 hour): 'Convert to the same unit first — 90 seconds vs 120 seconds for 2 minutes, and 3600 seconds for an hour.'
For the comparison item, ask the child to say WHY, not just pick an answer.

Accept converting to a common unit, or unit-size reasoning only when the number of larger units is at least as big as the number of smaller units (e.g. 20 minutes vs 30 seconds); for pairs like 90 seconds vs 1 minute, require conversion.
activities.rationale: Ordering and 'which is longer' items with mixed units are discriminating checks that reveal whether a child reasons about units or just the numbers. A recognition/selection or ordering format can be used for checking, but should follow the hands-on estimation and common-unit comparison work rather than replace it, since selecting a correct answer does not by itself elicit the felt calibration of estimating against a timer.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'estimate and read time with increasing accuracy to the nearest minute; record and compare time in terms of seconds, minutes and hours'.
learnerActions: Put a set of durations in order from shortest to longest: 90 seconds, 1 minute, 1 hour, 2 minutes (correct order: 1 minute, 90 seconds, 2 minutes, 1 hour).
Answer 'which is longer, 30 seconds or 20 minutes?' and explain the reasoning in units.
Match a list of events to their natural unit.
Estimate how long brushing teeth takes using a slider or spoken estimate, then check against a timer.
activities.intendedInsight: I can order and compare durations reliably by converting to a common unit and reasoning about unit size.

constraints: Reading, estimating and comparing are distinct strands — cover all three; precise reading alone does not address the estimation and comparison difficulties that carry the misconceptions.
A static 'how long does X take' poster can list useful benchmarks but cannot run the estimate-then-check calibration loop; use it as a reference, not as the estimation activity.
A character or spoken prompt can ask the child to estimate and compare, but needs a real timer alongside it for the too-fast-counter feedback to be felt.
The estimation error is a felt performance skill to rehearse against a real timer, not a concept to reteach by explanation.

Always make units explicit before comparing durations; never present a comparison item that rewards comparing bare numbers without their units, and never list the unit-blind answer (30 seconds longer than 20 minutes) as a correct option.
Recognition/selection and ordering items check whether a child reasons in units but do not by themselves elicit the felt calibration of estimating against a timer; pair them with hands-on estimation.
The dragging/common-unit-line and tap-to-reveal interactions are illustrative mechanisms; equivalent work with a stopwatch and a drawn number line on paper achieves the same objective.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claims '3D adds nothing' and that the errors are 'correctable only by a live feedback loop'; these are catalog-fit judgements, not established necessity claims. They have been softened to affordance-based statements (a real timer makes the estimation error felt; a static poster cannot run the loop; a sort checks classification but does not elicit the felt duration).

Self-audit of arithmetic/examples: 2:38 read as count-on from 35 (+3) is correct; 20 minutes = 1200 seconds is correct; 90 seconds vs 2 minutes = 120 seconds is correct (90s < 120s, so 2 minutes is longer); 1 hour = 3600 seconds; sequence order 1 minute (60s) < 90 seconds < 2 minutes (120s) < 1 hour (3600s) — all retained as learner-facing examples.

The 'count on from the last five' reading method and the 'discriminating check' framing come from the row pedagogy/White Rose scheme, not from a verbatim sources[].claim; the retained National Curriculum claim supports the objective of reading/comparing to the nearest minute, not the specific technique.

The 'later finish time means longer duration' misconception is noted in the original pedagogy as carried from earlier duration work; it is not directly targeted by these activities and may need a separate duration-difference activity if observed.

responseLevels.gap: Reads by counting single minutes; estimates wildly (counts too fast); compares durations by the bare number, ignoring units.
responseLevels.full: Reads to the exact minute, estimates short durations sensibly against a benchmark, and compares durations by converting to a common unit / reasoning about unit size, choosing appropriate units for events.
responseLevels.partial: Reads to the nearest minute and estimates roughly, but is caught comparing across units (30s vs 20min) or picking a sensible unit for unfamiliar events.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set estimating, reading and comparing tasks and WATCH: (1) Analogue clock at 2:38: 'Read this to the nearest minute and show me how.' (2) 'Close your eyes and put your hand up when you think 30 seconds has gone' — time it. (3) 'Which is longer — 30 seconds or 20 minutes? How do you know?' and 'About how long does it take to eat lunch — seconds, minutes or hours?' Watch the reading method, how far off the estimate is, and whether they reason about UNITS rather than just the numbers.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The '30 seconds vs 20 minutes' item is the classic unit-blind comparison probe: a child comparing bare numbers picks 30 seconds, a child reasoning about units picks 20 minutes. The eyes-closed estimate exposes the too-fast internal counter directly rather than by self-report.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Estimating volume
topic.description: Estimate volume of cuboids using 1 cm³ blocks; estimate capacity of containers using water
evidence: Build a cuboid from 1 cm³ blocks and state its volume
Estimate how many cm³ blocks would fill a given box
Estimate the capacity of a jug by comparing to known litre measures
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a small cardboard box, can they estimate how many 1 cm³ cubes would fit inside it — and then fill it with sugar cubes to check?

pedagogy.summary: Volume is the amount of three-dimensional space inside a solid, measured by packing it with unit cubes (each 1 cm³ = one cubic unit) with no gaps or overlaps and counting them. Children estimate and find the volume of a cuboid by building it from 1 cm³ blocks and seeing its LAYER structure — a layer holds rows×columns of cubes and the height tells how many layers — and connect packing with cubes to filling with liquid (a box holding 24 cm³ holds 24 ml of water). Packing volume is harder than area tiling because it demands 3-D spatial structuring.
bestPractices: Build cuboids from 1 cm³ cubes and watch the layers form; count as number-in-a-layer × number-of-layers.
Make hidden cubes explicit — the bottom layers you can't see still count; account for the whole 3-D array, not just the visible faces.
Estimate before packing (predict how many cubes fill the box), then check by building.
Connect packing to filling: pack a box with cm³ cubes and also fill it from a cylinder marked in ml, so 1 cm³ = 1 ml becomes real.
Use benchmark comparisons for capacity (compare a jug to a known 1-litre measure); state volume in cubic units.
keyRepresentations: A cuboid built from 1 cm³ cubes, decomposed into layers (rows × columns × layers)
The net of a box, used to predict the number of cubes to fill it
A box packed with cm³ cubes beside a graduated cylinder (1 cm³ = 1 ml)
A jug compared against a 1-litre benchmark for capacity estimation
commonMisconceptions: Counts only the visible cubes/faces and forgets the hidden lower layers — undercounting the 3-D array.
Adds the three dimensions (4+3+2) instead of building the layered array.
Treats the packed cubes as discrete objects, not as units of volume — doesn't see '24 cubes' as an amount of space.
Doesn't connect packing with filling — can't say how much water (ml) fills a box packed with 24 cm³ cubes.

learn.summary: Volume is the amount of 3-D space inside a solid, found by packing it with unit cubes (1 cm³ each) with no gaps or overlaps and counting them. Learners build a cuboid from 1 cm³ cubes, see its layer structure (a layer holds rows×columns of cubes; the height tells how many layers, so count = cubes-per-layer × layers), account for the hidden lower layers that cannot be seen, and connect packing with cubes to filling with liquid (a box packed with 24 cm³ holds 24 ml of water). Packing volume is harder than iterating length or tiling area because it demands extending spatial structuring from two to three dimensions.

activities.title: Pack a box layer by layer and reveal the hidden cubes
feedback: If a learner answers 12 ('the top is 4 by 3'), they have counted only the visible top layer. Have them physically lift the top layer to reveal the one beneath, then count number-in-a-layer × number-of-layers.

If a learner answers 9 ('4 + 3 + 2'), they are adding the three edges. Show that adding edges gives a length, not the space filled; pack the cubes to see it is layers of an array, so the dimensions multiply.
If a learner says just '24' meaning 24 loose blocks, name the unit: each block is 1 cubic centimetre, so the box holds 24 cm³ of space — the count measures volume, not a pile of objects.
If the box were twice as tall (4 layers instead of 2), ask how many cubes then and why — this checks whether the layer structure is secure (4 × 12 = 48).
activities.rationale: Decomposing a right rectangular prism into layers, each a rows-and-columns array, and recomposing multiplicatively (length×width cubes per layer, height = number of layers) is the targeted spatial structuring; predicting before packing surfaces undercounts based on the visible top or outer faces. Packing cubes physically lets learners rotate and open the solid to make the hidden interior cubes explicit.
sourceClaims: A unit cube (side length 1) has one cubic unit of volume; a solid figure packed without gaps or overlaps using n unit cubes has a volume of n cubic units (5.MD.3), and volume is measured by counting unit cubes in cubic cm/in/ft (5.MD.4). Packing volume is harder than iterating length or tiling area and demands extending spatial structuring from two to three dimensions.

Students decompose a right rectangular prism into layers, each a rows-and-columns array, and recompose multiplicatively — length×width gives the number of cubes in a layer and the height gives the number of layers; they may predict the number of cubes to fill a box from its net. Volume is additive.
learnerActions: Take an empty open box whose inside measures 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm and a pile of 1 cm³ cubes.
Before packing, predict how many cubes will fill the box completely and say WHY.
Lay the first layer as a 4-by-3 array and count it (12 cubes).
Stack the second layer on top and track the running count until it reads 24.
Rotate the box and open or lift the top layer to expose the bottom layer you could not see, confirming those hidden cubes still count.
State the count as cubes-per-layer × number-of-layers: 4×3 = 12 in a layer, 2 layers, 12×2 = 24.
State the result in cubic centimetres: 24 cm³.
activities.intendedInsight: Volume is a layered 3-D array: each layer holds rows×columns of cubes and the height gives the number of layers, so you multiply (or count layer by layer) and the hidden lower cubes count too. The answer is an amount of space measured in cubic units, not a heap of objects.

activities.title: Connect packing with cubes to filling with water
feedback: If a learner can count the cubes but cannot say how much water fills the box, move between filling and packing on the same container until 1 cm³ = 1 ml becomes visible.
If a learner treats '24 cubes' as discrete objects, re-ask what the unit of volume is, so '24' is read as 24 cm³ (= 24 ml) of space.
activities.rationale: A documented key difficulty is that learners who say a box holds 24 cubes often treat the 24 as individual objects, not units of volume, and cannot say how much liquid would fill it. Moving between filling and packing on the same container, with the 1 cm³ = 1 ml equivalence, targets exactly this disconnect.
sourceClaims: A key difficulty is the connection between 'packing' (cubes) and 'filling' (liquid): students who say a box holds 24 cubes often think of the 24 as individual discrete objects, not units of volume, and cannot confidently say how much liquid (from a cylinder marked in cc/ml) would fill the box. Instruction moves between filling and packing on the same container; 1 cm³ of water = 1 ml.
learnerActions: Pack the same box completely with 1 cm³ cubes and agree on the count (24).

Empty it, then fill it with water poured from a cylinder marked in millilitres (the box must be watertight, or use a watertight container with the same inside measurements), and read how much water was poured in.
Compare the two results: the cubes show the box holds 24 cm³, and the water reading should be about 24 ml (small differences come from measuring and filling errors).
State the equivalence in your own words: 1 cm³ of water = 1 ml, so 24 cm³ = 24 ml.
Answer: 'If I filled this box with water instead of cubes, about how much water would it hold? How does that relate to the cubes?'
activities.intendedInsight: Packing (cubes) and filling (liquid) describe the same amount of space: because 1 cm³ = 1 ml, a box whose inside is exactly filled by 24 one-centimetre cubes (24 cm³) holds 24 ml of water, and a real pour should give about 24 ml. The cube count is a measure of volume, not a tally of separate objects.

activities.title: Predict the cube count from a net
feedback: If the prediction ignores depth/layers, point to which dimension on the net gives the number of layers and rebuild to check.
If the prediction adds dimensions rather than multiplying, contrast an edge length with the filled space by packing one layer and stacking.
activities.rationale: The Progressions note that learners may predict the number of cubes to fill a box from its net; pairing a prediction with a physical build gives a discriminating check of layer structuring before the cubes are visible.
sourceClaims: Students decompose a right rectangular prism into layers, each a rows-and-columns array, and recompose multiplicatively — length×width gives the number of cubes in a layer and the height gives the number of layers; they may predict the number of cubes to fill a box from its net. Volume is additive.
learnerActions: Look at the flat net of a box before it is folded or packed.
Predict how many 1 cm³ cubes will fill the assembled box, explaining your reasoning in terms of a layer and the number of layers.
Fold/assemble (or build) the box and pack it to check your prediction.
Reconcile any difference between prediction and result, naming where the reasoning went wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: The layer structure can be read off a box's net before packing: identify the cubes in one layer (length×width) and how many layers (height), then multiply — and verify by building.

activities.title: Estimate a container's capacity against a benchmark
feedback: If an estimate is far off, re-anchor to the 1-litre benchmark and ask 'more than, less than, or about the same?' before pouring.
Encourage stating the result with a unit (ml or l) rather than a bare number.
activities.rationale: Benchmark comparison to a known 1-litre measure supports capacity estimation and extends the packing–filling link into everyday containers.
learnerActions: Pick a jug or container and estimate its capacity before measuring.
Compare it to a known 1-litre measure to judge whether it holds more or less, and roughly how much.
Pour to check against a graduated measure and state the capacity in millilitres or litres.
Relate capacity back to volume: discuss how a packed box's cm³ count would translate to ml.
activities.intendedInsight: Capacity can be estimated by comparison to a familiar benchmark (a 1-litre measure), and it connects to volume through the 1 cm³ = 1 ml relationship.

activities.title: Reference cutaway: the cubes you cannot see
feedback: If a learner still counts only visible faces, point to the cutaway's exposed lower layer and ask them to add those cubes to the total.
activities.rationale: A static cutaway makes explicit that hidden cubes count. This is a supporting scaffold: it clarifies hidden depth but does not let the learner pack, rotate, or fill, so it should accompany, not replace, hands-on packing.
learnerActions: Study a cutaway picture of a packed cuboid that shows the interior cubes, including the bottom layer.
Mark or count the hidden cubes that would be invisible from the outside.
Explain why the outside view alone undercounts the volume.
activities.intendedInsight: Unseen interior and bottom-layer cubes are part of the volume; relying on visible faces undercounts the 3-D array.

constraints: Learners must account for the whole 3-D array including hidden bottom layers, not just visible faces; make hidden cubes explicit by lifting/rotating or using a cutaway.
Estimate before packing or pouring, then check by building/measuring; prediction surfaces undercounts.
State volume in cubic units (cm³) and capacity in ml/l — a bare number is not enough; '24 cubes' should be read as 24 cm³ of space.
The static cutaway is a scaffold for the hidden-cubes idea only; it cannot support packing, rotating, or filling and should supplement hands-on work.

Hands-on paper/card models and cube sets have real thickness and can be picked up; treat the represented cuboid as an idealised mathematical solid and any zero-thickness on-screen diagram or flat picture as a model of that solid.

An on-screen layer builder with a live cube count and a pack-vs-fill-water toggle, or a grid layer × layer-count side view with a fill-with-water overlay, can make number-in-a-layer × layers and the cm³ = ml link concrete; these are optional illustrative mechanisms, not required ones. A flat side view does not directly display the hidden interior/bottom-layer cubes that packing real cubes or a cutaway reveals.
Recognition-only responses (e.g. choosing the right number) do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the layered count; have learners build, predict, and explain.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The 4×3×2 = 24 arithmetic, the single-layer distractor (12), and the add-the-edges distractor (9 = 4+3+2) were checked and are internally consistent; 48 for a doubled height (4 layers) also checks out.

The legacy 'conversation' entry was rated a poor fit with the claim that volume structuring is built by packing/filling 'not by in-role dialogue'. That comparative/necessity claim is not established by the sources; dialogue could still support reasoning. It has been omitted rather than restated as a universal law.
Capacity/benchmark estimation (jug vs 1-litre) is supported by the topic's stated evidence but has no directly supporting source claim, so its sourceClaims is [].

The cutaway activity's principle — that hidden/interior cubes count and visible faces undercount — is drawn from the stated common misconceptions, not from any sources[].claim, so its sourceClaims is []; the related 3-D structuring and layer-additivity claims are used in the packing activities instead.
The 1 cm³ = 1 ml equivalence and 'ml' content draw on the Grade 4 portion of the cited Progressions mirror as noted in the source.
An invented 'live recolouring' mechanism was removed from the constraints; only source-grounded optional mechanisms are retained.

assess.poeTask: Before packing, show the child the empty 4×3×2 box and the pile of 1 cm³ cubes and ask them to predict how many cubes will fill it completely and to say WHY. Then have them pack it, building layer by layer. The total of 24 confronts an under-prediction based on the visible top or the outside faces; the target explanation, given after packing, is that each layer holds 4×3 = 12 cubes and there are 2 layers.
probeDeeper: You can see the top of the box — how many cubes are underneath, in the layer you can't see? How do you know?
If the box were twice as tall — 4 layers instead of 2 — how many cubes then? Why?
If I filled this box with water instead of cubes, about how much water would it hold? How does that relate to the cubes?
Is your answer 24 cubes, or 24 of something else — what is the unit for volume?
assess.correctAnswer: 24 cubic centimetres. Each layer is a 4-by-3 array of 12 cubes and the box is 2 layers deep, so 12 × 2 = 24 (equivalently 4 × 3 × 2), counting the hidden lower layer as well as the top.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts one layer / visible cubes only: sees the top and forgets the box is layers deep, giving the single-layer count.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Extend the 2-D array to 3-D — build the box in layers, physically lift the top layer to reveal the one beneath; count number-in-a-layer × number-of-layers.
errorPatterns.distractor: 12 — the top of the box is 4 by 3, so 12 blocks.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 12 with 'the top has 4×3 = 12 blocks'; doesn't account for the second, lower layer.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the three dimensions instead of building the layered array (interference from length/perimeter thinking).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that adding the edges gives a length, not the space filled; pack cubes to see it is layers of an array, so the dimensions multiply.
errorPatterns.distractor: 9 — I added the three side lengths, 4 + 3 + 2.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 9 with '4 + 3 + 2'; treats volume like a sum of lengths.

errorPatterns.pattern: Packing–filling disconnect: can count the cubes but cannot say how much water would fill the box — hasn't connected packing (cubes) with filling (liquid).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pack the box with cm³ cubes and also fill it from a cylinder marked in ml on the same box, so 1 cm³ = 1 ml becomes visible.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the cube count but, asked how many ml of water fill the box, cannot connect it to the cubes (that it is 24 ml).

errorPatterns.pattern: Cubes as discrete objects, not units of volume: treats the answer as '24 blocks' with no cubic unit and no sense of it as an amount of space.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the unit — each block is 1 cubic centimetre, so the box holds 24 cm³ of space; the count measures volume, not a heap of objects.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says '24' meaning 24 loose blocks; omits the cubic unit and doesn't treat it as a volume.

responseLevels.gap: Counts only the visible top/faces or adds the dimensions; under- or mis-counts and shows no layer structure.
responseLevels.full: Finds volume as number-in-a-layer × number-of-layers (including hidden cubes), states it in cubic units, and connects packing with cubes to filling with liquid (24 cm³ = 24 ml).
responseLevels.partial: Finds the cube count for a built cuboid (by counting or multiplying) but the structure is fragile — forgets hidden layers on a harder case, or cannot connect the cube count to how much water the box holds.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a box that is 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm (or its net) and a pile of 1 cm³ blocks. Ask: 'How many 1 cm³ blocks are needed to fill this box completely — and how did you work it out?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The number alone can be reached different ways, so the reason tier carries it: a child with 3-D structure counts by layers (or multiplies) and accounts for hidden cubes; a child without it counts only the visible top/faces (undercounting) or adds the dimensions. A '24' justified by 'I counted the ones I can see' is caught.

sources.claim: A unit cube (side length 1) has one cubic unit of volume; a solid figure packed without gaps or overlaps using n unit cubes has a volume of n cubic units (5.MD.3), and volume is measured by counting unit cubes in cubic cm/in/ft (5.MD.4). Packing volume is harder than iterating length or tiling area and demands extending spatial structuring from two to three dimensions.

sources.claim: Students decompose a right rectangular prism into layers, each a rows-and-columns array, and recompose multiplicatively — length×width gives the number of cubes in a layer and the height gives the number of layers; they may predict the number of cubes to fill a box from its net. Volume is additive.

sources.claim: A key difficulty is the connection between 'packing' (cubes) and 'filling' (liquid): students who say a box holds 24 cubes often think of the 24 as individual discrete objects, not units of volume, and cannot confidently say how much liquid (from a cylinder marked in cc/ml) would fill the box. Instruction moves between filling and packing on the same container; 1 cm³ of water = 1 ml.

topic.name: Telling time to the minute (age 9+)
topic.description: Solve problems involving converting between units of time (hours↔minutes, minutes↔seconds, years↔months, weeks↔days)
evidence: A programme lasts 150 seconds — express in minutes and seconds
How many days are in 8 weeks and 3 days?
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to convert 2 hours 35 minutes into just minutes, can they do it — and then convert 180 seconds into minutes and seconds?

pedagogy.summary: Children convert between units of time — hours to/from minutes, minutes to/from seconds, years to/from months, weeks to/from days — including mixed quantities (3 hours 25 minutes = 3x60 + 25 = 205 minutes). The method is MULTIPLICATIVE (x60, x7, x12), using known number facts, and must resist the base-10 pull that assumes 100 seconds in a minute. The documented errors are additive rather than multiplicative reasoning, base-10 assumptions, and irregular groupings (months vary in length; a month is not exactly 4 weeks).
bestPractices: Use multiplicative reasoning with known facts (x60, x7, x12), not repeated addition
Convert mixed quantities in two parts: whole units x rate, then add the remainder (3x60 + 25)
Confront the base-10 pull explicitly: 60 seconds in a minute, not 100
Handle the reverse (150 s -> 2 min 30 s) by dividing and expressing the remainder
Flag irregular units — months vary; about 4 weeks in a month is approximate, not exact
keyRepresentations: Conversion tables (Days-Weeks, Years-Months, Minutes-Seconds)
The x60 / x7 / x12 rate as a known-fact chain (36 ÷ 6 = 6, so 360 s = 6 min)
A number track for counting leap years / weeks
A bar model splitting a mixed quantity into whole units + remainder
commonMisconceptions: Uses additive reasoning instead of multiplicative for conversions
Assumes base-10 (100 seconds in a minute, 100 minutes in an hour)
Thinks every month is exactly 4 weeks / all months are the same length
Converts a mixed quantity by ignoring the remainder or the second unit

learn.summary: Children convert between units of time — hours↔minutes, minutes↔seconds, years↔months, weeks↔days — including mixed quantities (e.g. 3 hours 25 minutes = 3×60 + 25 = 205 minutes). The core idea is MULTIPLICATIVE conversion (×60, ×7, ×12) using known number facts, and resisting the base-10 pull that wrongly assumes 100 seconds in a minute or 100 minutes in an hour. Reverse conversions require dividing and expressing the remainder (150 s → 2 min 30 s). Documented errors are additive rather than multiplicative reasoning, base-10 assumptions, mishandling the remainder/second unit in mixed quantities, and treating every month as exactly 4 weeks.

activities.title: Multiply-then-combine with a conversion machine
feedback: If a learner gives 180 minutes for 3 h 25 min, ask where the 25 minutes went; have them add the remainder back: 180 + 25 = 205. A bar model separating the whole units (3 × 60 = 180) from the remainder (25) can make the two-part split visible when the leftover is dropped.
If a learner reads 150 seconds as '1.5 minutes', group the seconds into sixties: two complete sixties and 30 left, so 2 minutes 30 seconds — 150 ÷ 60 = 2 remainder 30.
If a learner answers '2 minutes' for 150 seconds, point to the 30 seconds still unaccounted for and ask what happens to them.
If a learner uses ×100 for hours→minutes, contrast their answer with grouping into sixties so the 60-grouping is visibly correct.
activities.rationale: A visible multiply-then-add computation with a reverse divide-with-remainder makes the multiplicative structure and base-60 grouping concrete, directly confronting the additive and base-10 errors documented for this topic; the bar model scaffolds the whole-units-plus-remainder split.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y4 Time (Steps 1-2) documents that when converting units of time children may rely on additive rather than multiplicative reasoning, may assume base-10 (100 seconds in a minute / 100 minutes in an hour), and may think there are always exactly 4 weeks in a month; the method uses multiplicative reasoning and known number facts (e.g. 360 s = 6 min via the 6 times-table).

Children apply discrete whole-number, base-10 reasoning to time and cannot easily coordinate its non-standard groupings of 60, 12, 7, which underlies base-10 conversion errors and difficulty coordinating mixed units.
learnerActions: Take a mixed quantity such as 3 hours 25 minutes and convert it: multiply the whole units by the rate (3 × 60 = 180 minutes), then add the remaining 25 to get 205 minutes.
State out loud whether you counted up or multiplied, and why multiplying is faster.
Work a reverse conversion: take 150 seconds, group it into sixties — two full groups of 60 make 2 minutes, with 30 seconds left over, giving '2 minutes 30 seconds'.
Test the tempting '100 to a minute' idea against grouping real seconds into sixties, and describe what goes wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Converting units of time is multiply (by the fixed rate) then combine the remainder — not counting up — and for seconds, minutes and hours the grouping is 60, not 100.

activities.title: Known-facts conversion with a base-10 trap item
feedback: For '1.5 minutes', re-ground on 60: 1.5 of 60 would be 90 seconds, not 150; 150 seconds is 2 minutes 30 seconds.
For '2 minutes', ask about the leftover 30 seconds.
For 8 weeks 3 days, confirm 8 × 7 = 56 then add the 3 loose days for 59.
activities.rationale: Targeted items with carefully chosen wrong-answer options can help surface which error a learner is making (base-10 vs dropping the remainder vs additive). Such items check and may provoke reasoning; use them alongside worked construction, since choosing an answer does not by itself show the learner can carry out the method independently.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'solve problems involving converting between units of time'; the guidance adds pupils use all four operations in such problems, expressing answers appropriately (for example, days to weeks as weeks and days). Year 4 pupils 'solve problems involving converting from hours to minutes; minutes to seconds; years to months; weeks to days'.

Children apply discrete whole-number, base-10 reasoning to time and cannot easily coordinate its non-standard groupings of 60, 12, 7, which underlies base-10 conversion errors and difficulty coordinating mixed units.
learnerActions: Fill in conversions such as '3 h 25 min = ___ min' and show the multiply-then-add working.
Match a seconds amount (e.g. 150 s) to its minutes-and-seconds form.
Choose the correct reading of 150 seconds and explain why '1.5 minutes' (base-10 thinking) and '2 minutes' (dropped remainder) are both wrong.
Convert 8 weeks 3 days to days using 8 × 7 = 56, then + 3 = 59 days.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure conversions rest on known multiplication facts and on keeping the remainder; the common wrong answers to the 150-seconds item — '1.5 minutes' and '2 minutes' — correspond to base-10 thinking and to dropping the remainder.

activities.title: Irregular units: months, weeks and the calendar
feedback: If a learner converts months to days as ×28 or calls a month exactly 4 weeks, use the calendar to show months of 28, 30 and 31 days and distinguish the approximate month fact from the exact week-to-day fact.
activities.rationale: Addressing month-length variability with a concrete calendar directly targets the documented 'every month is exactly 4 weeks' misconception while keeping exact rates distinct from approximate ones.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y4 Time (Steps 1-2) documents that when converting units of time children may rely on additive rather than multiplicative reasoning, may assume base-10 (100 seconds in a minute / 100 minutes in an hour), and may think there are always exactly 4 weeks in a month; the method uses multiplicative reasoning and known number facts (e.g. 360 s = 6 min via the 6 times-table).

Year 5 pupils should 'solve problems involving converting between units of time'; the guidance adds pupils use all four operations in such problems, expressing answers appropriately (for example, days to weeks as weeks and days). Year 4 pupils 'solve problems involving converting from hours to minutes; minutes to seconds; years to months; weeks to days'.
learnerActions: Use a real calendar to count the days in several different months, including February, and record what you find: months have 28, 29 (February in a leap year), 30 or 31 days.
State why 'about 4 weeks in a month' is an approximation, not an exact conversion.
Contrast the exact fact (1 week = 7 days) with the approximate month fact, and explain how you would convert months to days versus weeks to days.
activities.intendedInsight: Some time units convert by exact fixed rates (7 days per week, 60 seconds per minute, 12 months per year) while month LENGTHS are irregular, so 'a month ≈ 4 weeks' cannot be used as an exact conversion to days.

activities.title: Pose-and-solve conversion word problems
feedback: Ask the learner to justify their chosen rate; if they add rather than multiply, prompt them to build the ×rate from a known fact.
Probe the remainder: 'Did you keep the leftover part, and where did it go in your answer?'
activities.rationale: Spoken or written word problems let a learner verbalise the method, which may expose additive-vs-multiplicative reasoning. On its own a spoken dialogue does not record whether the learner multiplied or added, so pair it with written working.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'solve problems involving converting between units of time'; the guidance adds pupils use all four operations in such problems, expressing answers appropriately (for example, days to weeks as weeks and days). Year 4 pupils 'solve problems involving converting from hours to minutes; minutes to seconds; years to months; weeks to days'.
learnerActions: Read or hear a word problem (e.g. 'A film lasts 150 seconds — how long is that in minutes and seconds?') and solve it, saying each step aloud.
Explain for each problem which rate you used (×60, ×7, ×12) and how you handled any remainder or second unit.
activities.intendedInsight: Conversions apply in context; choosing the right rate and correctly expressing mixed/remainder answers is part of solving the problem.

constraints: Use multiplicative reasoning with known facts (×60, ×7, ×12), not repeated addition; for mixed quantities convert whole units × rate, then add or keep the remainder.
Confront the base-10 pull explicitly: 60 seconds in a minute and 60 minutes in an hour, not 100; the 100-to-a-minute idea should be shown wrong against real grouping, not merely stated wrong.
Handle reverse conversions by dividing and expressing the remainder (150 s → 2 min 30 s), not rounding or dropping the leftover.
Keep exact rates (1 week = 7 days, 1 year = 12 months) distinct from the approximate month-to-weeks relationship; month lengths vary from 28 to 31 days.

Choosing a correct option in a matching or selection item checks reasoning but does not by itself demonstrate independent construction of the method; include tasks where the learner carries out and shows the conversion.
A fixed conversion poster or table can display the rates but does not let the learner compute and see the remainder form; treat it as a reference scaffold rather than the main activity.
A bar model (whole units + remainder) and a number track for counting weeks/leap years are optional representations that can scaffold the split and the counting, not required mechanisms.
Illustrative interactions (feeding units into a ×rate step, grouping seconds into sixties, a toggle offering the base-10 reading) are ways to make the mechanism visible, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic in the source was checked and is correct: 3 × 60 + 25 = 205 minutes; 150 ÷ 60 = 2 remainder 30 → 2 minutes 30 seconds; 8 × 7 + 3 = 59 days; 1.5 minutes = 90 seconds (so reading 150 s as '1.5 minutes' is genuinely wrong, as intended).

The source probe 'Is 90 minutes the same as 1.9 hours?' is a base-10 trap counterexample; the correct answer is that 90 minutes = 1.5 hours (since 60 minutes = 1 hour), not 1.9 hours. Retained only as a discussion prompt note, never as a learner answer option; any feedback must state 1.5 hours.

The original keyRepresentation 'number track for counting leap years / weeks' is retained as an optional scaffold in constraints and may be built into a dedicated activity where counting weeks or leap years is practised.

The source's assertions that '3D adds nothing' and that a static image or dialogue 'can't' teach the computation are catalog fit judgements, not established facts; they have been softened to scoped affordances/limits. Comparative efficacy or necessity of any single format is not established by the sources provided.

The sourceClaims on Activities 2 and 4 support the conversion content, the 'express answers appropriately' convention, and the documented errors, but do not validate the efficacy of selection/distractor items or spoken word problems; efficacy wording is kept conditional.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Unit relationships and conversion tables
topic.description: Know relative sizes of measurement units within one system (km/m/cm/mm, kg/g, l/ml, hr/min/sec); convert between different metric units and express measurements in terms of a smaller unit; record equivalents in conversion tables
evidence: Complete a conversion table for cm and mm: (1,10), (2,20), (3,30)...
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to convert 3.5 kg to grams, can they do it confidently — and also fill in a simple two-column table showing the same measurements in kg and g?

pedagogy.summary: Year 5 (age 9–10) pupils learn the relative sizes of metric units (km/m/cm/mm, kg/g, l/ml) and convert between them, expressing a measurement in terms of a smaller unit and recording equivalents in conversion tables. Conversion is APPLIED place value: to a smaller unit you multiply (there are more of them); to a larger unit you divide (fewer of them). The two persistent hazards are choosing the wrong operation and manipulating zeros/decimals mechanically ('add a zero') instead of moving the digits across a fixed decimal point.
bestPractices: Anchor the multiply/divide decision in REASONING about unit size, not a rule: 'which unit is bigger? there are fewer of the bigger unit, so to reach it I divide' — the rule is exactly what pupils reverse (Oak National Academy).

Teach conversion as multiplying/dividing by 10, 100, 1000, and talk about the DIGITS moving (one/two/three places) while the decimal point stays fixed — never 'move the decimal point' or 'add a zero' (NCETM Spine 2.29).
Secure fluency with ×/÷ by 10/100/1000 BEFORE layering on conversion, to avoid overload.
Use a place-value chart / Gattegno chart so pupils SEE the digits shift and the value change (the 1 in 1.75 km becomes the 1 thousand in 1750 m).

Build conversion tables and read them as a set of equivalent multiplications; include mixed-unit forms (2 kg 350 g = 2350 g) and always add a reasonableness check (bigger or smaller number than we started with?).
keyRepresentations: Place-value / Gattegno chart showing digits sliding across a fixed decimal point
Conversion tables (e.g. cm→mm: 1→10, 2→20, …)
Double number line linking two units
Bar showing a mixed unit (2 kg + 350 g) recomposed as one unit
commonMisconceptions: Confuses when to multiply and when to divide (converts to a smaller unit by dividing, or vice versa).
'Adds a zero' or manipulates zeros mechanically, which breaks with decimals (3.5 km → '350 m' or '3.50 m' instead of 3500 m).
Treats a mixed unit as concatenation (2 kg 35 g → '235 g'), a two-separate-numbers error.
Fills a conversion table by copying a pattern without understanding the ×10 relationship.

learn.summary: Year 5 pupils (age 9–10) learn the relative sizes of units within one system (metric km/m/cm/mm, kg/g, l/ml; and time units hr/min/sec, which are not metric) and convert between metric units, expressing a measurement in a smaller unit and recording equivalents in conversion tables. Metric conversion is applied place value: converting to a SMALLER unit means multiplying (there are more of them); converting to a LARGER unit means dividing (there are fewer of them). The two persistent hazards are choosing the wrong operation and manipulating zeros/decimals mechanically ('add a zero') instead of moving the digits across a fixed decimal point. The core activity is a live place-value transformation where digits slide across a fixed point, supported by table-building, mixed-unit recomposition, and targeted practice that probes direction and zero errors. (Note: the digit-sliding by 10/100/1000 applies to the metric units; hr/min/sec relate by ×60 and are included only in the 'relative sizes' knowledge.)

activities.title: Slide the digits across a fixed decimal point
feedback: If the pupil appends a zero (3.5 km → '3.50 m') or uses the wrong factor (3.5 km → '350 m', i.e. ×100), show the digits' positions on the chart: ×1000 moves each digit three places left past a fixed point, so 3.5 lands as 3500.
If direction is reversed (3.5 km → 0.0035 m), re-ask 'metres are smaller, so are there more or fewer than 3.5?' — more, so multiply, so the answer is bigger than 3.5.
Add a reasonableness check every time: 'Is your answer bigger or smaller than you started with, and does that fit the unit size?'
activities.rationale: Anchoring the multiply/divide choice in reasoning about unit size targets the exact rule pupils reverse, and showing digit movement across a fixed point addresses why 'add a zero' breaks with decimals. A live, interactive chart (type a value, choose a unit, see digits slide and point stay fixed) is proposed to make the transformation felt rather than told; a static reference table can show one worked conversion but does not let the pupil perform the operation or see the digits move.
sourceClaims: To multiply by 10/100/1000 the DIGITS move one/two/three places left (right to divide) while the decimal point stays fixed; measures are converted using multiplication and division by 10/100/1000; 'add/remove a zero' reasoning is false for decimals (e.g. 25.34×10 ≠ 25.340).
Pupils confuse when to multiply and when to divide when converting; the recommended fix is to reason about unit size — there are fewer of the larger unit, so converting to it means dividing.
learnerActions: Enter a measurement such as 3.5 km and choose the target unit (metres).
Before computing, answer the prompt: 'Is a metre bigger or smaller than a kilometre — so will there be MORE metres or FEWER?' State whether this means multiply or divide.

Watch (or physically move, using a place-value chart or Gattegno chart) every digit slide three places left while the decimal point stays nailed in place, so 3.5 becomes 3500, with place-holder zeros dropping in where needed.
Repeat for a case that keeps the decimal visible, e.g. 1.75 km to m, naming where each digit lands (the 1 becomes 1 thousand, giving 1750 m).
Do at least one divide case too, e.g. 4500 m to km, moving digits three places right to give 4.5 km.
activities.intendedInsight: The number grows (or shrinks) because the DIGITS move a fixed number of places, not because zeros are 'added' — so 3.5 km can never become 3.50 m.

activities.title: Build and check conversion tables
feedback: If a pupil pattern-copies without the ×10 idea, ask what single multiplication turns the left column into the right (auto-checking each row against ×10 makes a broken row visible immediately).
Correct answers for the cm→mm table: 1→10, 2→20, 5→50, 10→100.
activities.rationale: Reading tables as equivalent multiplications ties table completion back to the underlying factor, countering mechanical copying. Direction and factor practice map cleanly onto fill-in and matching tasks and can systematically probe the add-a-zero and direction errors, though such practice gives no live digit-movement.
sourceClaims: To multiply by 10/100/1000 the DIGITS move one/two/three places left (right to divide) while the decimal point stays fixed; measures are converted using multiplication and division by 10/100/1000; 'add/remove a zero' reasoning is false for decimals (e.g. 25.34×10 ≠ 25.340).
learnerActions: Complete a cm→mm table: 1→__, 2→__, 5→__, 10→__ and say what you multiply by for each row.
Read the completed table aloud as a set of equivalent multiplications ('each centimetre is ten millimetres — I'm multiplying by 10').
Check each row against the ×10 relationship and flag any row that breaks the pattern, explaining why it is wrong.
Build a second table for a different pair of units (e.g. kg→g, ×1000) to see the same structure with a different multiplier.
activities.intendedInsight: A conversion table is a repeated multiplication by the same factor, not a copied number pattern — understanding the factor lets you extend or correct any row.

activities.title: Recompose a mixed unit into one smaller unit
feedback: If the pupil concatenates (2 kg 35 g → '235 g'), show 2 kg = 2000 g on a place-value chart or bar and add 35, exposing the empty hundreds place: 2035 g.
Confirm 2 kg 350 g = 2350 g because 2000 + 350 = 2350 (the digits of 350 happen to fill all three lower places, which is why this case hides the error that 2 kg 35 g reveals).
activities.rationale: Mixed-unit concatenation is a whole-number 'two separate numbers' error; recomposing via place value and testing a case where the loose amount has fewer digits forces attention to the empty place-value columns.
sourceClaims: Children commonly treat a mixed measurement (or a decimal) as two separate whole numbers — e.g. '2 m and 30 cm' rather than 230 cm — driven by whole-number language.
learnerActions: Express 2 kg 350 g as a number of grams, showing the step 2 kg = 2000 g, then 2000 + 350 = 2350 g.
Test the tricky case 2 kg 35 g: decide whether it equals 235 g or 2035 g and justify using place value.
Use a bar (2 kg + loose grams recomposed as one quantity) to make the missing hundreds place visible when the loose amount is small.
State a check: the combined gram total must include the thousands from the kilograms.
activities.intendedInsight: A mixed unit is recomposed by converting the larger part and ADDING, not by writing the two numbers side by side — so 2 kg 35 g = 2035 g, not 235 g.

activities.title: Choose and justify the operation before calculating
feedback: If justification is only 'that's the rule', redirect to unit size: which unit is bigger, so are there more or fewer of the target unit?
For the true/false item: 25.34 × 10 = 253.4, NOT 25.340 — appending a zero does not multiply a decimal by 10; the digits move one place left.
activities.rationale: Requiring a stated justification before computing surfaces rule-guessing and builds the unit-size reasoning that fixes direction; true/false items on the zero error make the decimal failure explicit.
sourceClaims: Pupils confuse when to multiply and when to divide when converting; the recommended fix is to reason about unit size — there are fewer of the larger unit, so converting to it means dividing.

To multiply by 10/100/1000 the DIGITS move one/two/three places left (right to divide) while the decimal point stays fixed; measures are converted using multiplication and division by 10/100/1000; 'add/remove a zero' reasoning is false for decimals (e.g. 25.34×10 ≠ 25.340).
learnerActions: For a mix of conversions (some to smaller units, some to larger), first state 'multiply' or 'divide' and why, using unit size, BEFORE working the answer.
Answer true/false checks that target the zero error, e.g. 'Is 25.34 × 10 = 25.340?' and explain.
For each worked conversion, say aloud 'did I multiply or divide, and how did I know?'
activities.intendedInsight: The operation follows from which unit is bigger and how many of the smaller unit fit in it — the heuristic 'fewer of the bigger unit → divide' decides direction every time.

constraints: Secure fluency with ×/÷ by 10, 100 and 1000 BEFORE layering on conversion, to avoid overload.
Talk about the DIGITS moving one/two/three places while the decimal point stays fixed; never say 'move the decimal point' or 'add a zero'.

Practice tasks (fill-in conversions, matching equivalents, choose-the-operation items) are a strong companion for probing direction and zero errors but provide no live digit-movement feedback; pair them with the place-value chart work, which shows the transformation.
A static reference table or single worked example can show a result but does not let the pupil perform the conversion or watch digits move; treat it as reference only, not the main teaching vehicle.

A place-value slider/chart where digits visibly slide across a fixed point is proposed as a strong vehicle for THIS numeric transformation; it is not claimed superior for every topic. The content here is numeric, so 3D or spatial representations add little for this particular conversion skill.

Recognition-only responses (picking a correct conversion from options) do not by themselves show the pupil can independently reason about direction or move the digits; include tasks requiring them to produce and justify the conversion.

No arithmetic errors found in the migrated examples.

The original source listed one evidence-table row set as 1→10, 2→20, 3→30 while the assessment used 1,2,5,10 (→10,20,50,100); activities use 1,2,5,10 consistently. No conflict in the ×10 relationship, only in which rows are shown.

Some underlying sources were marked unverified (Oak National Academy guidance; DfE programmes of study) in the original row; their claims are retained as cited but their verification status is unchanged.

Per-activity sourceClaims were trimmed to those directly supporting each teaching principle: the general DfE 'pupils convert between metric units' claim and the Common Core 'convert / multi-step problems' claim were removed from activities where they supported only the topic, not the specific method taught.

All four original misconceptions are covered: direction confusion, 'add a zero', mixed-unit concatenation, and pattern-copying a table without the ×10 factor (the last via the table-builder's auto-check and the 'read the table as equivalent multiplications' action).
The double-number-line representation from the original keyRepresentations is not reflected in any activity; the bar model and place-value/Gattegno chart are used instead.

probeDeeper: 'Metres are smaller than kilometres — so should the number of metres be bigger or smaller than 3.5? Does your answer fit?'
'You wrote 3.5 km = ___ m. If I said 3.50 m, would that be right? Why not?'
'In your table, why does each centimetre become ten millimetres — what are you multiplying by?'
'Is 2 kg 35 g the same as 235 g? Show me on a place-value chart.'
assess.correctAnswer: 3.5 km = 3500 m (×1000, reasoning 'metres are smaller so there are more'); table 10, 20, 50, 100; 2 kg 350 g = 2350 g (2000 + 350). Chooses the operation from unit size and moves the digits correctly rather than appending zeros.

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiply/divide direction confusion — converts to a smaller unit by dividing (or to a larger unit by multiplying) because the operation is a memorised rule, not reasoning about unit size (e.g. 3.5 km → 0.0035 m).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reason from unit size every time: 'metres are smaller than kilometres, so there are MORE of them — multiply.' Rehearse the 'fewer of the bigger unit → divide' heuristic before any calculation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The answer is smaller when it should be bigger (or vice versa); the child cannot say why they multiplied or divided beyond 'that's the rule'.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Add a zero' / mechanical zeros — multiplies by 1000 by appending zeros, which breaks with the decimal: 3.5 km → '350 m' (one zero) or '3.50 m'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Switch to digit-movement on a place-value chart: to ×1000 the digits move three places LEFT past a fixed point; use true/false items (25.34×10 = 25.340?) to expose why 'add a zero' fails for decimals.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A converted value with the wrong number of digits after (or before) the point; zeros tacked on rather than digits moved three places.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mixed-unit concatenation — treats 2 kg 350 g as digits to string together, so a case like 2 kg 35 g becomes '235 g' instead of 2035 g (a two-separate-numbers error).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Recompose via place value: 2 kg = 2000 g, then add the loose grams; show 2 kg 35 g ≠ 235 g on a bar so the missing hundreds place is visible.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Recomposing a mixed unit by writing the two numbers side by side rather than adding 2000 g + 35 g.

responseLevels.gap: Guesses the operation, appends/removes zeros mechanically, and concatenates mixed units; a converted value with the wrong size.
responseLevels.full: Reasons from unit size to choose ×/÷, moves the digits correctly (including decimals) across a fixed point, recomposes mixed units into one smaller unit, and completes/reads conversion tables — transferring across length, mass and capacity.
responseLevels.partial: Converts a whole-number case in one direction but reverses direction the other way, mishandles the decimal in 3.5 km, or fills the table by pattern-copying without the ×10 idea.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child three tasks and ask them to think aloud: (1) 'Convert 3.5 km to metres.' (2) 'Complete this cm→mm table: 1→__, 2→__, 5→__, 10→__.' (3) 'Write 2 kg 350 g as a number of grams.' Each time ask 'did you multiply or divide, and how did you know?' Watch the direction reasoning and how they handle the digits/zeros — not just the answers.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A pupil who understands converts 3.5 km to 3500 m and justifies by unit size; a pupil who doesn't either divides (0.0035 m) or 'adds a zero' (350 m / 3.50 m), and may concatenate 2 kg 350 g wrongly for a case like 2 kg 35 g. Reasoning-from-unit-size versus rule-guessing diverge exactly on the direction and on the decimal case.

pedagogy.summary: Year 6 (age 10–11) pupils convert between standard units using DECIMAL notation to up to three decimal places, moving in both directions (smaller↔larger), and can explain the mm–cm–m–km (and g–kg, ml–l) relationships as powers of 10. This is the decimal extension of Year 5 conversion: the same 'reason from unit size, move the digits' method, now with the decimal point in play. The load-bearing hazard is decimal place value — the 'add/remove a zero' shortcut fails (3250 g ÷ 1000 is 3.25 kg, not 325), and children who think 'the point is the decimal' misplace digits.
bestPractices: Convert by moving the DIGITS across a fixed decimal point (×/÷ by 10/100/1000), explicitly rejecting 'add a zero' and 'move the point' — use true/false error-spotting (0.45÷10 = .45?) to confront the shortcut (NCETM Spine 2.29).
Keep the unit-size reasoning from Year 5 ('larger unit → fewer → divide') so direction is reasoned, not guessed.
Make the powers-of-10 STRUCTURE explicit: 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1000 m = 1 km — so a conversion is one multiplication/division by a power of ten, and mixed chains compose.
Use a place-value chart extended to thousandths so pupils can state the value of each digit before and after, and place holder zeros correctly.
Include a reasonableness check (should the number get bigger or smaller?) to catch direction and decimal-placement errors.

learn.summary: Year 6 pupils (age 10–11) convert between standard measurement units using decimal notation to up to three decimal places, moving in both directions (smaller↔larger), and explain the mm–cm–m–km (and g–kg, ml–l) relationships as powers of ten. This extends Year 5 conversion with the decimal point now in play: the method stays 'reason from unit size, then move the DIGITS across a fixed decimal point', using ×/÷ by 10/100/1000. The load-bearing hazard is decimal place value — the 'add/remove a zero' shortcut fails (3250 g ÷ 1000 = 3.25 kg, not 325), and children who think 'the point is the decimal fraction' misplace digit values.

activities.title: Move the digits, keep the point still (place-value conversion)
feedback: If a learner answers 325 kg for 3250 g, they removed zeros instead of moving digits three places. Rebuild it on the chart: 3250 ÷ 1000 moves each digit three places right, giving 3.25 — count the places, do not delete symbols.

If a learner answers 4.5 m or 45 m for 0.45 km, name the error precisely: 4.5 m is a one-place shift (as if ×10), and 45 m is a two-place shift (as if ×100). Both are wrong; 0.45 × 1000 moves digits three places left to 450 m. Have them name the value of the 4 (four tenths) and the 5 (five hundredths) first, then shift three places.
If an answer is wildly out (e.g. 0.00045 m or 3 250 000 kg), the multiply/divide direction was reversed. Re-reason from unit size before trusting the result.
If a learner treats 0.45 as the whole number 45, rebuild decimal place value: each column to the right is ten times smaller, so 0.45 is four tenths and five hundredths.
activities.rationale: Converting by moving digits across a fixed point directly confronts the 'add/remove a zero' shortcut, which fails for decimals; pairing it with explicit unit-size reasoning keeps direction reasoned rather than guessed, and the equal-value check (3.250 = 3.25) addresses holder-zero confusion. The 5 cm→0.05 m case instances the same method on a shorter chain.

learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart extended to thousandths. Write 3250 g in it, then convert to kilograms by sliding every digit three places to the RIGHT (dividing by 1000) while the decimal point stays fixed, landing on 3.25 kg; note that a holder zero is inserted only where place value demands it.
Before moving, state the unit-size reason aloud: 'Kilograms are the bigger unit, so there will be FEWER of them — I divide.' Then check the direction of the digit shift matches.
Convert the reverse case 0.45 km to metres (×1000), sliding digits three places LEFT to get 450 m; state that metres are smaller, so there are MORE.

Convert 5 cm to 0.05 m (÷100), sliding each digit two places to the right — a shorter example of the same digit-movement method with decimal notation; say why metres are the larger unit so there are fewer.
Confirm that 3.250 kg and 3.25 kg name the same quantity — the trailing zero after the last significant digit does not change the value.
Do a reasonableness check each time: 'Should this number get bigger or smaller?' and reject any answer that is orders of magnitude out.
activities.intendedInsight: A conversion moves the SAME digits across a FIXED decimal point; the point does not move. Converting to a larger unit gives fewer of them (divide, digits move right); converting to a smaller unit gives more (multiply, digits move left). 3250 g and 3.25 kg are one quantity; 3.250 equals 3.25.

activities.title: Spot the false shortcut (error-spotting with decimals)
feedback: If a learner accepts 0.45 ÷ 10 = .45, show on the chart that dividing by ten moves each digit one place right: 0.45 → 0.045. Nothing was divided in '.45'.
If a learner accepts 25.34 × 10 = 25.340, point out that 25.340 equals 25.34 (same value). Multiplying by ten gives 253.4 — digits move one place left.
activities.rationale: True/false error-spotting on carefully chosen decimal cases makes the failure of the zero shortcut explicit and forces articulation of digit movement and place value.
sourceClaims: Convert measures by moving the DIGITS across a fixed decimal point via ×/÷ by 10/100/1000; the guide embeds 'add/remove a zero' as FALSE statements for decimals (0.45÷10 = .45; 25.34×10 = 25.340) to expose the misconception.
A common decimal misconception is thinking 'the point is the decimal fraction'; place value must extend so each column to the right is ten times smaller, and holder zeros are understood.
learnerActions: Judge true or false and explain: 'Is 0.45 ÷ 10 = .45?' Correct it to 0.045 by moving each digit one place right.
Judge true or false: 'Is 25.34 × 10 = 25.340?' Explain that appending a zero after the last decimal does NOT multiply by ten; the correct answer is 253.4, with digits moving one place left.
For each false statement, state the correct conversion and justify it with the value of each digit and the direction of movement.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or removing a zero is not the same as multiplying or dividing by a power of ten once decimals are involved. ×/÷ by 10, 100, 1000 moves the digits by one, two, or three places; the zero trick coincidentally works for some whole numbers but misvalues decimals.

activities.title: Climb the powers-of-ten ladder (composing conversions)
feedback: If a learner cannot say why 1 km = 1000 m, walk the ladder rung by rung (m → ×10 → tens of metres → ×10 → hundreds → ×10 → 1000 m) so the ×1000 is seen as 10×10×10.
If a learner treats g–kg differently from m–km, point out both are ÷1000 (or ×1000) — the same power-of-ten structure applies.
activities.rationale: Making the powers-of-ten structure explicit lets conversions be reasoned and composed rather than memorised, which supports transfer across length, mass and volume.
sourceClaims: UK DfE Year 6 pupils solve problems involving conversion of units using decimal notation up to three decimal places, converting length/mass/volume/time from a smaller unit to a larger and vice versa.
A common decimal misconception is thinking 'the point is the decimal fraction'; place value must extend so each column to the right is ten times smaller, and holder zeros are understood.
learnerActions: Build a ladder stating each relationship: 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1000 m = 1 km. For each rung, say whether you multiply or divide and by what power of ten.
Hop along the ladder to compose a chain, e.g. mm → cm (÷10) → m (÷100) → km (÷1000), and recognise that any single conversion is one multiplication or division by a power of ten.
Optionally use a Gattegno chart (rows for powers of ten) to see each conversion as a single ×/÷ by a power of ten — moving along a row, or jumping rows for the larger steps.
Explain in words why 1 km is a thousand metres and not a hundred, using the powers-of-ten structure rather than reciting it as an isolated fact.

Transfer the same structure to mass (g–kg) and volume (ml–l) to show the method is general across metric units, not tied to length. Then contrast with time (e.g. 2.5 h = 150 min, not 250 min) to see that time units use factors of 60 and 24, not powers of ten.
activities.intendedInsight: The metric system is built on powers of ten, so every metric conversion is a single ×/÷ by a power of ten and mixed chains compose; knowing the structure removes the need to memorise each conversion separately. Time units are not decimal (60 s = 1 min, 60 min = 1 h, 24 h = 1 day), so time conversions use those factors instead of powers of ten.

constraints: Reject 'add/remove a zero' and 'move the decimal point' as methods; teach movement of the DIGITS across a point that stays fixed.
Keep unit-size reasoning ('larger unit → fewer → divide; smaller unit → more → multiply') so direction is reasoned, not guessed, and pair it with a reasonableness check.

A fixed reference ladder of powers of ten can show the relationships but does not let a learner move digits or check direction themselves; use it alongside an activity where the learner performs the transformation (chart, writing, or spoken step-by-step), not as the only medium.

Matching, fill-in-the-blank and multiple-choice items (including true/false decimal cases) can probe direction and the add-a-zero error precisely, but recognition responses do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the conversion; include tasks where the learner produces the converted value and justifies it.
Ensure a holder zero is inserted only where place value requires it (e.g. 0.045), and that trailing zeros after the last significant decimal (3.250 vs 3.25) are recognised as equal value.

An extended place-value chart to thousandths, a double number line between the two units, and a Gattegno chart for ×/÷ by powers of ten are useful supports but are scaffolds; learners should also reason and state values without them to show secure understanding.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3250 g ÷ 1000 = 3.25 kg (digits move three places right); 0.45 km × 1000 = 450 m (three places left); 5 cm ÷ 100 = 0.05 m (two places right); 0.45 ÷ 10 = 0.045 (one place right); 25.34 × 10 = 253.4 (one place left, NOT 25.340). All checked and consistent with the source's intended corrections. The misconception answers (325 kg, 45 m, 4.5 m, 25.340, 0.00045 m, 3 250 000 kg) appear only as errors to correct, never as valid answers.

The original source frames an interactive place-value slider as 'ideal' and a static image/3D/dialogue as 'poor' for this topic. These are catalog fit rankings, not established comparative efficacy; this rewrite retains the digit-movement mechanism as a concrete support while softening claims that other media 'cannot teach' the concept. A static ladder, Gattegno chart, and spoken/written reasoning can also support the objective.
The Gattegno chart from the original keyRepresentations is retained as an optional scaffold in the powers-of-ten activity and the scaffold constraint.
One listed source (DfE National Curriculum) carries verified:false in the row; treat its claim with appropriate caution pending verification.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Add/remove a zero' with decimals — divides 3250 by 1000 by deleting zeros ('325 kg'), or multiplies 0.45 by 1000 by appending/one-step zeros ('45 m' or '4.5 m').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Move digits three places on a place-value chart with the point fixed; use true/false items (0.45÷10 = .45? 25.34×10 = 25.340?) to show the zero shortcut fails for decimals.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The answer has the wrong number of decimal places; zeros were added/removed rather than digits moved three places.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the multiply/divide direction — gives an answer orders of magnitude out (0.45 km → 0.00045 m, or 3250 g → 3 250 000 kg).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reason from unit size first ('metres smaller → more → multiply') and add a reasonableness check before trusting the answer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The result is far bigger/smaller than sensible; no unit-size reasoning offered.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The point is the decimal' — mis-values digits after the point, treating 0.45 as the whole number 45 or misreading thousandths.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild decimal place value: each column right is ten times smaller; state the value of each digit in 0.45 (four tenths, five hundredths) before converting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Digit values after the point are wrong; 0.45 handled as 45; three-decimal-place answers misplaced.

responseLevels.gap: Adds/removes zeros, reverses direction, or mis-values decimal digits; answers orders of magnitude out.
responseLevels.full: Converts both directions with correct decimal placement (digits move, point fixed), handles up to 3 dp, and explains the ×/÷ powers-of-10 structure linking mm–cm–m–km — transferring across length, mass, volume and time.
responseLevels.partial: Converts a friendly case correctly but slips on three decimal places or on the reverse direction, or converts but cannot explain the powers-of-10 relationship.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to think aloud through three tasks: (1) 'Convert 3250 g to kilograms.' (2) 'Convert 0.45 km to metres.' (3) 'Explain how mm, cm, m and km are related using powers of 10.' Watch the direction choice, where the decimal point ends up, and whether the powers-of-10 structure is understood — not just the final numbers.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A pupil with secure decimal place value moves the digits the right number of places in the right direction (3.25 kg; 450 m) and explains the ×10 chain; a pupil relying on 'add/remove a zero' produces 325 kg or 45 m, and one who thinks 'the point is the decimal' mis-values 0.45.
